technology.title: The one password I used for everything (and why I stopped)
technology.desc: What The Tech? with Your Mate MattLet me own up to something first. For years I used one password for just about everything. Email, Facebook, banking, the lot. It was a good password too. Capital letter and a number and everything. Most of us have done the same, because who can remember forty different logins?Here's why I stopped, and why it's worth five minutes of your time.Every so often a big website gets hacked. Not you, not anything you did, just some online shop or forum you signed up to a decade ago. The email addresses and passwords in there end up on a list, and that list gets sold to the highest bidder. Then software goes down the list trying those same details everywhere else: email, Facebook, the banks, Xero, MYOB. It's completely automated.There's no hacker singling anyone out, a computer is just trying the same key in every door it can find. And the door that matters most is email. Think about what happens when you forget a password: the reset link lands in your inbox. So whoever controls the inbox can reset their way into nearly everything else. Your email password isn't one key on the ring. It's the key to the ring.The good news is the fix is quick and free.First, give your email a password it shares with nothing else. The strongest and easiest kind is three or four random words stuck together. Something like "jetty paddock biscuit tuesday" takes centuries to crack and ten seconds to remember, and it beats anything built from a pets name and postcode.Second, turn on two-factor authentication for your email and your banking. Scary name, simple thing: when there's a login from a new device, a code gets sent to your phone, and without the code the password alone is useless. Every email provider and bank offers it, usually under security settings, and it takes five minutes. If a password ever does leak, this is what stops it mattering.Third, sort the rest however suits you. A password manager (an app that remembers them all behind one strong master password) is the tidy option, and the good ones are free or close to it. Even a notebook in a drawer at home works.That's the one job for this fortnight. New password on the email, code on the phone for email and banking. Twenty minutes, costs nothing, and it quietly closed the biggest gap I had in my own setup.Stuck on where the settings live? Give me a yell and I'll point you at the right menu.Matt Rowlands runs Your Mate Agency, helping regional businesses get found online. Get in touch at yourmateagency.com.au or 0478 101 521.

world.title: AMECEA PLENARY: “Church Structures Exist, but Gaps Remain,” Young People’s Concern at AMECEA Plenary
world.desc:
Sr. Jecinter Antoinette Okoth, FSSA
In their message to the Bishops of the Association of Member Episcopal Conferences in Eastern Africa (AMECEA) during the 21st Plenary Assembly, young people highlighted that while the Catholic Church has put in place structures to involve them in its life and mission, significant gaps continue to limit their genuine participation.
In a submission read to hundreds of delegates on Wednesday, July 22, youth representative Ms. Hayat Abdi from Ethiopia acknowledged the Church's efforts to create spaces for their engagement, including youth chaplaincies, animators at various levels, and dedicated avenues for youth representation.
We appreciate collaborative spaces created to involve the youth, she said and pointed out that the existence of these structures has not translated into meaningful involvement since the existing frameworks are “often under-resourced, difficult to access, and slow to translate into real influence over decisions that shape young people’s lives in the Church.”
According to the young people, the message shared with the Bishops was an extensive, region-wide consultation that began in Zambia in 2024, when the AMECEA Secretariat convened a forum of youthful leaders from across the region.
A follow-up meeting in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania, in 2026 led to a region-wide data-collection exercise, which gathered views from thousands of young people through national conversations, webinars, and virtual interactions.
The youth representatives from all the member conferences assured Bishops that this process ensured their submission reflected voices in a representation that is true, deep, and meaningful.
Despite these concerns, youth delegates expressed gratitude for being included in the Synodal process itself, calling it an assurance that the Church desires to not only speak to us the young people, but to walk with us as companions on the journey of faith, the Ethiopian Catholic youth read in parts.
She described themselves as the present, vibrant and active church, committed to her mission, but at a critical stage of transition seeking trust, guidance, and room to contribute as full participants rather than passive recipients of pastoral care.”
The young people therefore appealed for stronger structures within the broader challenges they face, including: unemployment, poverty, mental health struggles, and political exclusion.
The youths further highlighted creativity, digital literacy, and adaptability of young people as resources the Church can draw on.
world.source: Association of Member Episcopal Conferences in Eastern Africa
